constitutive_assumptions: Bending deformation occurs exclusively at the primary shape of the conductive TPU between the two electrodes; other substrate sections are assumed rigid enough to resist deformation.
The top layer length of the conductive TPU remains constant during bending due to the inextensible layer, inducing compressive strain in the bottom volume.
The electrical conductivity of conductive TPU is assumed to be directly proportional to the volume fraction of carbon black particles within the primary shape.
The conductive TPU resistance is inversely proportional to carbon black volume fraction and directly proportional to cross-sectional area.
Each bending joint segment is modeled as an elastic cantilever beam with small deflection angles where sin(alpha_i) is approximated by alpha_i.
The silicone rubber pneumatic actuator is approximated as a linear elastic beam within small strain under zero internal air pressure, with fiber reinforcement neglected in stiffness calculations.
Conductive TPU elastic modulus change with temperature is assumed negligible across the 20–50 °C test range because its glass transition temperature is below 0 °C.
control_variables: Operational temperature interval during bending and position sensing (Tl = 40 °C to Tu = 50 °C, centered around Tg = 45 °C)
Electrical heating power (0.75 W from DC power supply)
Geometric dimensions of the finger (L0 = 20 mm, L1 = 40 mm, L2 = 20 mm, Ltotal = 115 mm, primary shape thickness t = 2.5 mm, length l = 5 mm)
Displacement evaluation range for stiffness calculation (0 to 0.8 mm linear interval)
FDM 3D printing parameters (SMP nozzle 220 °C, conductive TPU nozzle 240 °C, platform 30 °C, layer thickness 0.3 mm, 100% infill)
Material formulations (SMP MM-4520 with Tg = 45 °C; PI-ETPU 95-250 carbon black composite; VeroClear 950 mold material)
dependent_variables: External force at the fingertip under applied displacement (N)
Conductive TPU electrical resistance / voltage (Ohms / V)
Fingertip reference point E spatial coordinates (x, y)
Heating time to reach glass transition temperature (seconds)
Cooling time / heat dissipation rate from 50 °C to Tg (seconds)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Soft robotic fingers achieve variable stiffness by modulating shape memory polymer (SMP) temperature around its glass transition temperature using embedded conductive TPU heaters, exhibiting an 8.18-fold stiffness change at zero air pressure.
Conductive TPU elastomer performs dual roles within a soft finger joint as an embedded Joule heating element and a piezoresistive strain sensor for position estimation.
Concurrent fused deposition modeling (FDM) 3D printing produces an interlocking multi-material substrate of SMP and conductive TPU in a single setup without assembly.

A theoretical model relating primary shape volume/cross-section changes of conductive TPU to carbon black volume fraction predicts electrical resistance variation consistent with experimental results up to 90 degrees of joint bending.
Preheating conductive TPU/SMP joints to 35 °C reduces thermal activation time from room temperature (40 s) to under 10 s with 0.75 W power input.
Passive convective ventilation features integrated into the finger substrate accelerate cooling, reducing cooling duration from 50 °C to 45 °C from 30 s to 15 s when increasing ventilation area.
Increasing pneumatic actuator air pressure increases overall baseline finger stiffness and reduces the relative stiffness modulation ratio achieved by thermal SMP modulus changes.
Optical tracking of fingertip reference point coordinates closely matches kinematic predictions derived from conductive TPU joint resistance measurements across pneumatic pressures from 0 to 100 kPa.

experimental_setup: Dual-nozzle fused deposition modeling (FDM) 3D printer modified with an auxiliary cooling system to concurrently print SMP (MM-4520, Tg = 45 °C) and conductive TPU (PI-ETPU 95-250) into an interlocking substrate.

Two-stage molding process utilizing VeroClear 950 molds (Objet260 Connex1) to fabricate the silicone rubber pneumatic chamber, apply inextensible layer and fiber reinforcement, and encapsulate the multi-material substrate.
Thermal characterization setup comprising an FLIR SC660 thermal imaging camera, Keysight E36105A DC power supply, and an infrared thermometer (-50 °C to 380 °C, precision ±1.5 °C).

Piezoresistive measurement circuit cascading the conductive TPU joint with a known reference resistor, monitored via an Arduino Nano and a 24-bit ADS1256 ADC under rigid-shell joint isolation across bending angles from 30° to 180°.

Stiffness measurement apparatus consisting of a motor-driven horizontal linear screw guide (0 to 5 mm displacement at 0.2 mm increments), vertical linear guide, digital force gauge (0–10 N, precision 0.01 N), and SMC AR20-01-A pressure regulator testing at 0, 50, and 100 kPa.
Optical position feedback tracking setup using an HD camera capturing reference point E coordinates across pressures from 0 to 100 kPa at 45–50 °C.
future_work: Testing position feedback repeatability and assessing cyclic fatigue/lifespan of SMP and conductive TPU over hundreds or thousands of cycles.
Investigating the material and physical mechanisms underlying the divergence between theoretical predictions and experimental resistance at bending angles greater than 90°.
Implementing closed-loop temperature control (e.g., using embedded thermocouples) without compromising finger compliance or stiffness.
independent_variables: Joint temperature (room temperature 20 °C vs. heated state 50 °C; preheat from 35 °C to 45 °C)
Pneumatic actuation air pressure (0 kPa, 50 kPa, 100 kPa; 0 to 100 kPa in 20 kPa steps)
External displacement applied at fingertip (0 to 5 mm in 0.2 mm increments)
Joint bending angle (30° to 180° in 30° increments)
Ventilation feature surface area (three sizes: A1, A2, A3)
limitations_inferred: The analytical stiffness model is restricted to zero pneumatic pressure and does not capture stiffening behavior under combined pneumatic pressurization and thermal state changes.
Thermal transition times (10 s heating with preheating, 15 s cooling) limit dynamic response rates and real-time stiffness modulation bandwidth.
Position feedback validation was performed quasi-statically at discrete pressure steps without evaluating dynamic grasping, external payload disturbances, or obstacle contacts.
Inherent piezoresistive elastomer drift and thermal cross-sensitivity may degrade calibration stability over prolonged operation without frequent baseline calibration.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Heating time from ambient room temperature (20 °C) to 45 °C is approximately 40 s, which is too long for practical applications without preheating.
Ventilation feature dimensions cannot exceed critical bounds without risking physical separation of conductive TPU from the substrate during bending.
Theoretical resistance modeling diverges substantially from experimental measurements at bending angles greater than 90 degrees due to unmodeled material effects.
Joint bending angles must be restricted to a maximum of 90 degrees in practice to maintain estimation accuracy.
Joint temperature was controlled within a band (45–50 °C) rather than a precise setpoint, introducing thermal drift and measurement variability in resistance.
Embedding thermocouples for closed-loop thermal control without altering finger compliance and stiffness remains an unresolved challenge.
Long-term position feedback repeatability and operational cycle life of SMP and conductive TPU have not yet been evaluated across extended cycles.
Simplifications in theoretical stiffness modeling (cantilever beam approximation and neglecting fiber reinforcement) caused quantitative discrepancies with experimental force measurements.
main_results: Direct dual-material FDM 3D printing successfully fabricated an interlocking SMP and conductive TPU substrate in a single setup without assembly.
Conductive TPU heaters achieved localized Joule heating above Tg (45 °C) using 0.75 W power in less than 10 s when preheated to 35 °C (40 s from 20 °C).
Increased ventilation opening area reduced cooling time from 50 °C to Tg (45 °C) from ~30 s (area A3) to ~15 s (area A1).
At zero air pressure, finger stiffness decreased from 0.18 N/mm below Tg (20 °C) to 0.022 N/mm above Tg (50 °C), yielding a stiffness variation ratio of 8.18.
Increasing pneumatic pressure raised overall stiffness and lowered the relative stiffness ratio between thermal states due to actuator elastomeric stiffness dominating at elevated pressures.
Conductive TPU resistance decreased monotonically with joint bending angle, aligning closely with theoretical predictions up to 90° before deviating at higher angles.
Tip positions estimated via conductive TPU resistance closely tracked direct visual measurements across 0–100 kPa pneumatic actuation pressures.
modeling_methods: Kinematic modeling of multi-joint finger bending using geometric coordinate transformations for fingertip position tracking.
Piezoresistive analytical modeling linking joint bending angle to conductive TPU cross-sectional area and carbon black volume fraction changes.
Structural stiffness modeling treating substrate bending joints as composite elastic cantilever beams under fingertip load.
Linear elastic beam modeling of the unpressurized silicone rubber actuator cross-section for baseline bending stiffness.
performance_metrics: Stiffness modulation ratio (8.18 at 0 kPa pressure; kl1 = 0.18 N/mm vs. kh1 = 0.022 N/mm)
Heating duration (40 s from 20 °C to 45 °C; <10 s from 35 °C to 45 °C at 0.75 W)
Cooling duration from 50 °C to 45 °C (15 s for ventilation area A1; 30 s for A3)
Resistance prediction fidelity up to 90° bending angle
Visual vs. sensor-derived coordinate tracking accuracy for fingertip reference point E
possible_gap_implications: A 10–15 s thermal response time may prevent applications requiring rapid, adaptive stiffness switching during dynamic grasping tasks.
Limiting joint bending to 90° to avoid resistance modeling errors restricts the kinematic grasping envelope of the finger.
Lack of closed-loop temperature control and potential sensor drift may hinder precise position and force regulation in uncalibrated or changing ambient thermal conditions.
Absence of a combined electromechanical-pneumatic model limits model-based control of variable-stiffness soft actuators under simultaneous inflation and thermal modulation.
paper.research_objective: To achieve both compliance controllability (variable stiffness) and position feedback in soft robotic fingers through a multi-smart-material 3D-printed substrate combining shape memory polymer and conductive thermoplastic polyurethane integrated with a soft pneumatic actuator.
paper.research_problem: Soft robotic fingers and grippers have limited ability to modulate compliance over a wide range to balance conformability and load capacity, and face challenges integrating compact, non-rigid heating and position sensing without sacrificing compliance and contact safety.
stiffness_mechanism: thermally tuned elastic modulus change around glass transition temperature (Tg)
paper.title: Novel Variable-Stiffness Robotic Fingers with Built-In Position Feedback
